author: A Robot
objectives: Determine steric number from a Lewis structure by counting bonding pairs and lone pairs as electron domains.
Predict electron-domain geometry from steric number using VSEPR theory.
Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry when lone pairs are present.
Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs and how this compresses bond angles.
Apply VSEPR predictions to real molecules including CO2, BF3, CH4, NH3, H2O, PF5, SF6, and XeF4.

modules.moduleName: Scene 1: VSEPR Setup and Lewis Structure Input
modules.description: Introduces the core idea of VSEPR theory and shows how a flat Lewis structure is used to predict 3D molecular shape.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: State the central VSEPR principle that electron domains arrange to minimize repulsion.
Count electron domains from a Lewis structure, including bonds and lone pairs.
Recognize that Lewis structures are 2D representations while molecular geometry is 3D.
instructions: Look at the central atom and the reference Lewis-structure panel.
Use the narration to connect the flat drawing to the 3D prediction task.

components.text: Central atom
VSEPR Theory: Electron domains repel and spread out

H-O-H with 2 lone pairs
Count domains around O: 4

Each bond = 1 domain
Each lone pair = 1 domain
Double/triple bonds still count as 1 domain
VSEPR Theory: Shapes arise from electron-pair repulsion

clips.changeMeaning: Updates the opening title panel to foreground the repulsion principle, focusing student attention on the big idea before examples appear.
clips.narration: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory, or VSEPR, starts from a simple idea: electron domains around a central atom repel one another and arrange themselves as far apart as possible in three-dimensional space.

clips.changeMeaning: Brings the Lewis structure and counting rule panels into focus so students can connect a flat diagram to electron-domain counting.
clips.narration: We usually begin with a Lewis structure, which is drawn flat on paper. Around the central atom, each single bond, double bond, triple bond, and each lone pair counts as one electron domain.

components.text: O central atom

Water, H2O
2 O-H bonds + 2 lone pairs = 4 domains

clips.changeMeaning: Refines the labels to the specific water example so students can practice identifying the central atom and steric number from the Lewis structure.
clips.narration: In water, oxygen is the central atom. It has two bonding domains and two lone-pair domains, for a total steric number of four. VSEPR uses that count to predict the three-dimensional arrangement.

modules.moduleName: Scene 2: Minimum Repulsion with 2, 3, and 4 Domains
modules.description: Shows electron domains moving apart into linear, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral arrangements as more domains are added.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Relate increasing numbers of electron domains to specific minimum-repulsion geometries.
Identify the ideal angles for linear, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral arrangements.
Visualize electron-domain repulsion as the cause of geometric reorganization.
instructions: Watch the electron clouds reposition as new domains are added.
Notice how the geometry name and ideal angle update after each rearrangement.

components.text: 2 domains → Linear, 180°
2 domains → Linear, 180°

clips.changeMeaning: Moves two initially offset domains into opposite directions and briefly displays a repulsion indicator to demonstrate the linear minimum-repulsion arrangement.
clips.narration: With two electron domains, the farthest-apart arrangement is straight across the central atom. The domains settle 180 degrees apart, giving a linear electron-domain geometry.

components.text: 3 domains → Trigonal planar, 120°

clips.changeMeaning: Adds a third domain and redistributes all three into a planar triangular pattern, illustrating how geometry changes when repulsion must be minimized among three domains.
clips.narration: When a third domain is added, the linear arrangement is no longer optimal. The three domains spread into a trigonal planar arrangement, separated by ideal angles of 120 degrees.

components.text: 4 domains → Tetrahedral, 109.5°

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces a fourth domain and repositions the set into a three-dimensional tetrahedral pattern so students can see the first nonplanar VSEPR geometry.
clips.narration: With four domains, the best arrangement is tetrahedral. The domains point toward the corners of a tetrahedron, producing the familiar ideal angle of about 109.5 degrees.

modules.moduleName: Scene 3: Five and Six Domains plus Geometry Summary
modules.description: Extends the geometry catalog to trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral arrangements and concludes with a summary panel of all five electron-domain geometries.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral electron-domain geometries from steric numbers five and six.
Differentiate axial and equatorial positions in trigonal bipyramidal geometry.
Summarize the full set of five fundamental electron-domain geometries and their ideal angles.
instructions: Observe how the fifth and sixth domains change the arrangement.
Use the summary panel to compare all steric numbers and ideal angles.

components.text: 5 domains → Trigonal bipyramidal

2 Linear 180°
3 Trigonal planar 120°
4 Tetrahedral 109.5°
5 Trigonal bipyramidal 90°/120°
6 Octahedral 90°

5 domains → Trigonal bipyramidal
3 equatorial, 2 axial

clips.changeMeaning: Reinforces the five-domain arrangement by labeling equatorial and axial positions, helping students interpret the mixed 90 and 120 degree angles.
clips.narration: A fifth domain produces trigonal bipyramidal geometry. Three domains occupy equatorial positions in one plane, while two take axial positions above and below that plane.

components.text: 6 domains → Octahedral, 90°

clips.changeMeaning: Adds the sixth domain and reorganizes the domains into six equivalent directions, illustrating the octahedral minimum-repulsion arrangement.
clips.narration: With six domains, the arrangement becomes octahedral. The six directions are equivalent, and neighboring domains are separated by 90 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: Shows a consolidated summary chart and leaves the model available for free viewing so students can compare all five geometries against the listed steric numbers and angles.
clips.narration: Together, these are the five fundamental electron-domain geometries in VSEPR theory: linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral. The steric number determines which arrangement is predicted.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4: Electron-Domain Geometry versus Molecular Geometry
modules.description: Compares methane, ammonia, and water to show how lone pairs preserve electron-domain geometry while changing molecular shape.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Differentiate electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry.
Predict molecular geometry from a tetrahedral electron-domain arrangement containing zero, one, or two lone pairs.
Explain why lone pairs are counted for electron-domain geometry but not seen as atoms in molecular geometry.
instructions: Compare the labels before and after bonded atoms are replaced by lone pairs.
Focus on which parts count toward electron-domain geometry and which parts define molecular geometry.

components.text:
CH4
Electron-domain geometry: tetrahedral
Molecular geometry: tetrahedral

CH4
Electron-domain geometry: tetrahedral
Molecular geometry: tetrahedral

clips.changeMeaning: Begins with methane, where all four tetrahedral positions are bonding domains, so the electron-domain and molecular geometries are identical.
clips.narration: Methane has four bonding domains and no lone pairs on carbon. Because all four tetrahedral positions are occupied by bonds, the electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry are both tetrahedral.

components.text:
NH3
Electron-domain geometry: tetrahedral
Molecular geometry: trigonal pyramidal

clips.changeMeaning: Replaces one bonded atom with a lone-pair cloud while keeping the underlying four-domain arrangement, highlighting the shift from tetrahedral to trigonal pyramidal molecular shape.
clips.narration: Now replace one bonding domain with a lone pair. In ammonia, nitrogen still has four electron domains total, so the electron-domain geometry remains tetrahedral. But the atoms alone trace out a trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry.

components.text:
H2O
Electron-domain geometry: tetrahedral
Molecular geometry: bent

clips.changeMeaning: Replaces a second bonding domain with another lone pair, showing water’s bent molecular geometry while the tetrahedral electron-domain geometry persists.
clips.narration: In water, oxygen has two bonding domains and two lone pairs. The underlying electron-domain geometry is still tetrahedral, but the molecular geometry, based only on the atom positions, is bent.

modules.moduleName: Scene 5: Lone Pairs and Bond-Angle Compression
modules.description: Displays methane, ammonia, and water side by side to explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space and compress bond angles.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare ideal tetrahedral and observed bond angles in methane, ammonia, and water.
Explain why lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs.
Predict that increasing lone-pair count decreases adjacent bond angles.
instructions: Compare the labeled bond angles across the three molecules.
Notice the larger lone-pair clouds in ammonia and water and relate them to angle compression.

components.text: More lone pairs → smaller bond angle

clips.changeMeaning: Updates the comparison panel to emphasize the measured bond angles for the three tetrahedral-domain molecules, setting up a clear trend.
clips.narration: Compare these three molecules with the same underlying tetrahedral electron-domain geometry. Methane has the ideal tetrahedral angle of 109.5 degrees, ammonia is slightly smaller at about 107 degrees, and water is smaller still at about 104.5 degrees.

components.text: Lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs

clips.changeMeaning: Enlarges the lone-pair clouds to visually encode their greater spatial demand, helping students connect electron density distribution to stronger repulsion.
clips.narration: Lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs. Because they are attracted by only one nucleus instead of being shared between two nuclei, their electron density spreads out more and pushes neighboring bonds closer together.

components.text: Overlay view: bond angle decreases as lone pairs increase

clips.changeMeaning: Enables an overlay comparison view so students can directly compare the angle compression trend at a shared center point.
clips.narration: In the overlay view, the pattern is easier to see: as lone pairs replace bonding pairs around a tetrahedral center, the remaining bond angle becomes progressively compressed.

Relate steric number and lone-pair count to observed 3D structure.
Use representative molecules to validate VSEPR predictions against real examples.
instructions: Move your view among the molecule gallery.
Compare each 3D model with its Lewis-structure label and geometry annotation.

clips.changeMeaning: Uses the top-row examples to map one representative molecule onto each fundamental electron-domain geometry, reinforcing the geometry catalog with real compounds.
clips.narration: These molecules provide representative examples of the five electron-domain geometries: carbon dioxide is linear, boron trifluoride is trigonal planar, methane is tetrahedral, phosphorus pentafluoride is trigonal bipyramidal, and sulfur hexafluoride is octahedral.

components.text: Lone pairs modify molecular geometry: NH3, H2O, XeF4

clips.changeMeaning: Shifts emphasis to lone-pair-containing examples and enlarges them slightly to highlight how molecular geometry differs from the electron-domain arrangement.
clips.narration: These additional examples show how lone pairs change the molecular geometry. Ammonia is trigonal pyramidal, water is bent, and xenon tetrafluoride is square planar even though its electron-domain geometry is octahedral.

components.text: For each molecule: count domains, identify ED geometry, then name molecular geometry

clips.changeMeaning: Concludes the gallery with a procedure prompt that connects each displayed example back to the VSEPR reasoning sequence students should internalize.
clips.narration: For each molecule, the reasoning process is the same: count the bonding and lone-pair domains around the central atom, determine the electron-domain geometry, and then name the molecular geometry from the positions of the atoms.

modules.moduleName: Scene 7: Prediction Activity — Drag the Domains
modules.description: Students conceptually arrange electron domains into correct VSEPR geometries, including an example with a lone pair in a tetrahedral arrangement.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Predict the correct spatial arrangement for 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 electron domains.
Recognize that lone pairs occupy electron-domain positions even when not part of the visible molecular shape.
Connect geometry prediction to angular criteria used for correctness.
instructions: Imagine dragging the domains to maximize separation around the central atom.
Notice the confirmation label when the arrangement matches the target geometry.

components.text: Challenge: Arrange 4 domains
Challenge 1: 4 domains → tetrahedral

clips.changeMeaning: Sets up the first challenge using four electron domains around the center, directing attention to the tetrahedral target arrangement.
clips.narration: In this prediction activity, imagine dragging the domains until repulsion is minimized. With four domains, the correct arrangement is tetrahedral.

components.text: Confirmed: tetrahedral arrangement

clips.changeMeaning: Moves the initially loose domains into the correct tetrahedral positions and confirms the geometry, modeling how the system would validate a correct arrangement.
clips.narration: When the domains are placed close to the correct tetrahedral angles, the configuration snaps into its idealized arrangement.

components.text: Other challenge targets: 2 linear, 3 trigonal planar, 5 trigonal bipyramidal, 6 octahedral

clips.changeMeaning: Expands the challenge scope to the full set of domain counts so students connect each steric number to a geometry target.
clips.narration: The same approach works for other steric numbers as well: two gives linear, three gives trigonal planar, five gives trigonal bipyramidal, and six gives octahedral.

components.text: Mixed case: 4 domains with 1 lone pair → ED geometry tetrahedral, molecular geometry trigonal pyramidal

clips.changeMeaning: Replaces one electron domain with a lone pair to show that the tetrahedral electron-domain positions remain relevant even when the visible molecular geometry changes.
clips.narration: A mixed case requires a second layer of reasoning. Four total domains still occupy tetrahedral positions, but if one is a lone pair, the molecular geometry traced by the atoms becomes trigonal pyramidal.

modules.moduleName: Scene 8: Prediction Activity — Pick the Correct Geometry
modules.description: Uses unfamiliar Lewis structures and candidate models to practice VSEPR prediction by counting domains and accounting for lone pairs.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Determine steric number and lone-pair count from a Lewis structure.
Choose the correct molecular geometry from candidate 3D structures.
Justify geometry choices using the sequence count domains, identify electron-domain geometry, account for lone pairs.
instructions: Read each Lewis structure prompt and compare the candidate 3D shapes.
Use the reasoning sequence shown in the explanation panel after each reveal.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces SF4 and updates the panels with explicit domain counting, guiding the student to the correct electron-domain geometry before molecular shape selection.
clips.narration: For sulfur tetrafluoride, count four bonding domains and one lone pair around sulfur. That gives a steric number of five, so the electron-domain geometry is trigonal bipyramidal.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the correct candidate model and states the full reasoning chain from steric number to molecular geometry for SF4.
clips.narration: Because one equatorial position is occupied by a lone pair, the molecular geometry of SF4 is seesaw.

components.text: More prompts: ClF3 → T-shaped, BrF5 → square pyramidal, I3- → linear
Use the same steps each time: count domains, identify ED geometry, account for lone pairs, then name the molecular geometry

clips.changeMeaning: Generalizes the exercise to additional unfamiliar molecules and reinforces the reusable VSEPR reasoning algorithm across multiple steric numbers.
clips.narration: The same logic extends to other molecules. Chlorine trifluoride is T-shaped, bromine pentafluoride is square pyramidal, and triiodide is linear once you count domains and account for lone pairs correctly.

modules.description: Closes the lab by revisiting the major concepts in sequence and linking them into a complete VSEPR prediction workflow.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Summarize the five major concept areas covered in the lab.
Recall the complete VSEPR workflow from Lewis structure to predicted 3D shape.
Integrate electron-domain geometry, lone pairs, and real-molecule examples into one framework.
instructions: Follow the highlighted summary items as the narration reviews the full workflow.
Use this final scene to mentally rehearse the prediction sequence.

components.text:
1. Minimum repulsion principle
2. Five electron-domain geometries
3. Electron-domain vs molecular geometry
4. Lone-pair angle compression
5. Real molecules and prediction practice
Workflow: Lewis structure → count domains → ED geometry → account for lone pairs → molecular geometry

clips.changeMeaning: Begins the recap by positioning the highlight bar at the first concept area, cueing a structured review of the lab topics.
clips.narration: Let’s review the main ideas. VSEPR begins with the minimum-repulsion principle: electron domains arrange themselves to stay as far apart as possible.

components.text: Five ED geometries: linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral

clips.changeMeaning: Moves the visual emphasis to geometry classification and updates the workflow panel to consolidate the five electron-domain geometries.
clips.narration: From the steric number, you identify one of five electron-domain geometries: linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, or octahedral.

components.text: Final rule: molecular geometry depends on atom positions only, but lone pairs still shape the arrangement and compress bond angles

clips.changeMeaning: Concludes by emphasizing the distinction between electron-domain and molecular geometry, tying lone-pair effects into the complete prediction workflow.
clips.narration: Finally, remember that molecular geometry is named from the atom positions, not the lone pairs. But lone pairs still occupy space, alter the electron-domain arrangement, and often compress bond angles from their ideal values.
